forces: Soprano, English horn and concert band
performers: Susan Kavinski, soprano; Richard Reed, English horn; United States Navy Concert Band
intro: Mahler’s “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen”, from the Rückert-Lieder, is heard here in an arrangement for concert band, performed by Susan Kavinski with the English-horn soloist Richard Reed and the United States Navy Concert Band. The singer has withdrawn from a world that may think her dead, and lives in love and song.

cues.title: Opening, English horn
cues.text: The English horn opens with a quiet rising phrase, with long spaces between the notes. Mahler marks the opening extremely slow and restrained. Richard Reed is the instrumental soloist, and his melody is the one Susan Kavinski later sings to the first words.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Rückert-Lieder, orchestral score, printed pp. 15–16: cor anglais opening and ruhevoll vocal entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/eb/IMSLP22552-PMLP47682-Mahler_-_R%C3%BCckert_Lieder_(orch._score).pdf. Recording credits: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Ich_bin_der_Welt_abhanden_gekommen%22_from_R%C3%BCckert-Lieder_-_United_States_Navy_Band.ogg. The concert-band arranger and score are unidentified; tempo and vocal details here come from Mahler’s orchestral score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First draft, Maiernigg, 1901
cues.text: Mahler dated the first draft 16 August 1901, at Maiernigg by the Wörthersee. He wrote the song in the summer before he met Alma.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, essay on Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen, autumn 2008, dates the draft and places it before Mahler’s meeting with Alma: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596

cues.title: Vocal entry, rehearsal 1
cues.text: “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen”: I have slipped away from the world. Kavinski takes up the English horn’s melody, marked “ruhevoll” (peaceful). Rückert’s first stanza explains a long absence.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 16–17, rehearsal 1: vocal entry and Friedrich Rückert’s first stanza. Our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fuga between voice and bass
cues.text: At “mit der ich sonst viele Zeit verdorben” (with which I once wasted so much time), voice and bass move in a ‘fuga’, the old rhetorical figure of flight. Their rhythms are offset. Reinhold Kubik read this as tempus fugit, the loss of time itself.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition work introduction to the Rückert-Lieder (autumn 2008): a “fuga” (“flight”) between voice and instrumental bass at these words, the offsetting of rhythms expressing the loss of time itself, “tempus fugit”: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596

cues.title: Second stanza
cues.text: The singer has not been heard from by the world, which may suppose her dead, and she is content that it should think so. At rehearsal 4, marked Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen, Mahler gives the second stanza a little more movement. The vocal line stays close to the rhythm of speech.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 18–21: end of Rückert’s first stanza, second stanza and Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen at rehearsal 4.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: English horn phrase, rehearsal 6
cues.text: The voice stops after “gestorben der Welt” — dead to the world. During the vocal rest the English horn plays a rising phrase heard earlier in the song. The passage, at rehearsal 6, is marked Wieder zurückhaltend, and the tempo slows again before the last stanza.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 22–23, rehearsal 6: Wieder zurückhaltend and the cor anglais phrase during the vocal rest. Our translation of Rückert’s words.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final stanza, Tempo I
cues.text: “Und ruh’ in einem stillen Gebiet”: and rest in a quiet place. The opening tempo returns, and the voice enters low. Rückert’s final stanza moves from the world’s commotion to the singer’s own heaven, love and song.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 23–24: Tempo I, low vocal entry and Rückert’s final stanza. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final lines, rehearsal figures 7–8
cues.text: “Ich leb’ allein in meinem Himmel” — I live alone in my heaven. Mahler marks the voice “innig” — intimate — and “Ohne Steigerung”, without increase, as the line reaches “Himmel”. The words “in meinem Lieben” — in my loving — are sung twice before the final mention of song.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 24, rehearsal figures 7–8: innig, intimo, Ohne Steigerung, Senza aumentare and repeated words. Rückert’s words as set by Mahler; our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Manuscript for Guido Adler, 1905
cues.text: Mahler gave Guido Adler the orchestral manuscript for his fiftieth birthday in 1905, writing on the title page that he hoped he would “never lose” his friend. Under the Nazis Adler lost his library and titles. The manuscript, thought lost, resurfaced when a lawyer’s son tried to sell it.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition work introduction to the Rückert-Lieder (autumn 2008): Mahler presented the manuscript of the orchestral version to Adler on his 50th birthday in 1905, with a title-page dedication that he hoped he “would never lose” his friend; under the Nazi regime Adler lost his library and titles, and the manuscript, thought lost, came to light when the son of a lawyer tried to sell it: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596

cues.title: Final vocal phrase and close
cues.text: Kavinski’s last words are “in meinem Lied” (in my song). The English horn continues and takes up the singer’s rising phrase. Mahler marks the final notes morendo, and the closing chord is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 25, rehearsal 9: final vocal words, cor anglais return, morendo and the final fermata. Our translation. The band arrangement’s individual accompaniment parts are not documented.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: English horn phrase passes to soprano
transitions.to: A · Voice enters with opening melody
transitions.how: The soprano’s low entrance repeats the English horn’s opening phrase. “Ich bin der Welt” moves at the same tempo, marked ruhevoll.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 15–16, rehearsal 1. The concert-band recording credits Kavinski and Reed as the two soloists; the arrangement score is unavailable.

transitions.title: First stanza into Etwas fließender
transitions.from: A · Voice enters with opening melody
transitions.how: At the end of the first stanza the word “gestorben” is stretched across several notes. The next line begins more freely at Etwas fließender, with the words “Es ist mir auch gar nichts daran gelegen”. In Mahler’s orchestral score this change comes between rehearsal figures 3 and 4, marked Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 18–19, rehearsal figures 3–4: vocal phrase and Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen. Accompaniment scoring is not transferred to the band arrangement.

transitions.title: The English horn returns between stanzas
transitions.to: Link · The English horn holds back
transitions.how: The voice repeats “Gestorben” before coming to rest on “der Welt”. The English horn returns in the silence that follows. Wieder zurückhaltend slows its rising phrase before the opening tempo returns.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 22–23, rehearsal 6: repeated vocal word, cor anglais and Wieder zurückhaltend. The original score supplies the structural reference for this band version.

transitions.title: Soprano re-enters at Tempo I
transitions.from: Link · The English horn holds back
transitions.how: The English horn finishes its phrase and the soprano begins low at Tempo I. The opening words, “Ich bin”, are repeated and now lead to “gestorben dem Weltgetümmel” (dead to the world’s commotion). The vocal line then rises.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 23: Tempo I and the third stanza’s vocal line. Our translation of Rückert’s words as set by Mahler.

transitions.title: Vocal close and English horn return
transitions.to: Coda · English horn after the voice
transitions.how: The voice ends the final “Lied” on a long note. The English horn then plays the singer’s rising phrase. Mahler marks the closing pages morendo, and the last chord is held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 25, rehearsal 9: vocal close, cor anglais return, morendo and final fermata. The band’s redistribution of the accompaniment is undocumented.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified
fields.note: Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
